title: Larry's Partner

jokes.text: Hank's announcer intro: 'and me, "hey, now!" Hank Kingsley' — inserting himself into the guest list as if he's equal billing with Marisa Tomei, Pete Rose, and Anne Rice
jokes.setup: Hank reads the standard guest list — Marisa Tomei, Pete Rose, Anne Rice — legitimate celebrity guests
jokes.punchline: He appends himself to the list as if he belongs there, complete with his catchphrase as a credential
jokes.explanation: Pure Hank — his delusional self-aggrandizement compressed into one sentence. The joke only works because of Tambor's specific character; a different sidekick doing the same thing wouldn't land. The 'hey, now' as a credential is a beautiful detail. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Air force major general Harold campbell
dialogue.line: described president clinton as gay-loving, pot-smoking, and womanizing.

dialogue.speaker: Clinton
dialogue.line: Well, at least I'm fun to be with.

jokes.text: Hank's announcer intro: 'and now, because only he contains a touch of pure creamery butter, Larry Sanders!'
jokes.setup: Standard late-night announcer intro building to the host's entrance
jokes.punchline: 'because only he contains a touch of pure creamery butter' — a completely random, meaningless non-sequitur inserted where a genuine superlative would go
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it weaponizes the formal pomposity of late-night announcer-speak against itself. The phrase 'pure creamery butter' is perfectly specific in its absurdity — it sounds like ad-copy from a dairy commercial grafted onto a human being. It's also character comedy: only Hank, a man of magnificent self-delusion and hollow showbiz grandiosity, would write this for his own show intro and deliver it without irony. Strong originality and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Pepsi is attempting to control the damage caused by recent tampering by switching to a brand-new slogan, which is 'diet pepsi-- even with a syringe, it's just one calorie.'

jokes.text: Clinton retaliated by saying, 'Well, at least I'm fun to be with.'
jokes.setup: Air Force Major General described Clinton as 'gay-loving, pot-smoking, and womanizing'
jokes.punchline: Clinton's imagined comeback owns all three charges as a positive — reframing vices as charm
jokes.explanation: Solid topical monologue joke — the structure is clean, the misdirection works (you expect a denial, get an embrace). Dated by the Clinton-era politics but the construction is professional. Stand-up content.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: She wasn't wearing underwear, was she? Ha ha! That shook you up, didn't it? You were very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Damn right, it shook me up. I stunk the rest of the show.

jokes.text: 'Diet Pepsi — Even with a syringe, it's just one calorie.'
jokes.setup: Pepsi dealing with a tampering scare, switching to a new slogan
jokes.punchline: The new slogan spins the tampering as a feature, not a bug — the syringe becomes the vehicle for calorie counting
jokes.explanation: Probably the strongest monologue joke — the fake slogan format is brilliantly economical, the pivot from scandal to diet-brand logic is genuinely clever. Low character integration because it's generic topical stand-up, but as a joke construction it's tight.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I did 12 jokes. I laughed at all 12. Well, that means she didn't laugh 9 times.

jokes.text: Artie: 'She wasn't wearing underwear, was she?' / Larry: 'That shook you up, didn't it?' / Larry: 'I stunk the rest of the show.'
jokes.setup: Post-show debrief — everyone praising Larry's performance with Marisa Tomei
jokes.punchline: Artie's leering question reveals that the whole staff noticed, and Larry's honest admission that it derailed him is self-deprecating gold
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders character beat — the show-within-a-show mechanics (the actual performance affecting Larry's mental state) combined with Artie's bawdy older-man energy. The admission 'I stunk the rest of the show' is both honest and pathetic in a funny way.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A once-talented nobody who obviously wants something from someone.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I did 12 jokes.' / Unknown: 'I laughed at all 12.' / Larry: 'Well, that means she didn't laugh 9 times.'
jokes.setup: Someone reassures Larry by claiming to have laughed at all 12 jokes
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately does the math to find failure — of the 12 jokes, someone didn't laugh at 9, so he zeroes in on the negative
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes — Larry Sanders' defining neurosis in mathematical form. Someone assures him of perfect success and he immediately recalculates it as evidence of failure. Only Larry Sanders could deliver this line; it's character-specific, perfectly structured, instantly quotable, and requires zero setup beyond knowing who Larry is. Justifies the 8.5 score easily — comparable to the 8.0 anchor in economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You want me to kick his parasitic ass into the street?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What is your problem?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's right. I forgot. You used to be a bouncer.

jokes.text: Larry's agent always calls when he's on the air — 'He'll call you back.' / 'Yeah, he'll call me tomorrow night when I'm on the air.' / 'Trick him. Put him through tomorrow.'
jokes.setup: Beverly notes Larry's agent called during the show
jokes.punchline: The agent apparently only ever calls during show time — then the solution is to 'trick' the agent by putting him through while Larry's on air again
jokes.explanation: A quick industry joke — Hollywood agent behavior satirized neatly. The 'trick him' solution is a fun escalation but the overall joke is functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Jeez, not a day goes by we don't think, 'Hey-- what-- where's Stan?'

jokes.text: Larry describes his ex-partner Stan as 'a once-talented nobody who obviously wants something from someone'
jokes.setup: Beverly announces a Stan Paxton is waiting downstairs
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate, bitchy character assassination — 'once-talented nobody' is a perfectly constructed insult
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'once-talented nobody' is genuinely sharp — it's a contradiction that works, and the added 'who obviously wants something from someone' shows Larry's show-business cynicism in crystalline form. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: Turn around, let me see the ass.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: No. Let me see the-- come on, let me see the ass.

jokes.text: Artie offers to 'kick his parasitic ass into the street' before immediately catching himself: 'That's how I started in show biz — sometimes I revert, ok?'
jokes.setup: Artie reacts to hearing Stan's name with aggressive hostility
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Artie was a bouncer — delivered deadpan as if it explains everything — is a perfect character detail
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's Artie is the show's secret weapon and this is a perfect Artie moment — the sudden violence followed by the sheepish self-awareness is very funny. 'Sometimes I revert, ok?' is a great line. High character integration because this is only funny coming from the gravelly, dangerous Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: I was jerking off the other day. Steam came out.

jokes.text: Stan to Larry: 'So do you — a little older maybe. Turn around, let me see the ass.'
jokes.setup: Stan and Larry exchanging pleasantries, 'you look great'
jokes.punchline: Stan immediately pivots to inspecting Larry's ass, treating it as a legitimate physical assessment — the intimacy of old friends landing awkwardly in a professional setting
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe moment — the old-friend overfamiliarity against the formal backdrop of a TV studio. Larry's discomfort ('No. No.') and Stan's obliviousness are good character work, but the joke itself is fairly standard.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: It's a check for $127 that I owe you.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: For what?

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: 1978, baltimore Holiday inn. You were sleeping. I took $127 out of your pocket.

jokes.text: Stan: 'I was jerking off the other day. Steam came out.' / Artie: 'I've had that happen too.'
jokes.setup: Stan making an aging joke about the encounter with Larry after 15 years
jokes.punchline: Artie's deadpan 'I've had that happen too' — he takes the joke completely literally and one-ups it, implying he's so old this has actually happened
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Artie's deadpan acceptance of the absurdist premise — not laughing along, not batting it away, but confirming it as personal experience — is both character-perfect and genuinely surprising. The economy is remarkable: one short sentence does all the work. Justifies the 8.3 score. Rip Torn's delivery would make this legendary.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What did you need the money for?

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: I don't know. Coke, hookers--something. At least it didn't go to waste.

jokes.text: Stan to Artie: 'I wish you could see your eyebrows. Really. They're—'
jokes.setup: Artie is being his usual gruff self
jokes.punchline: Stan can't even finish the sentence — the eyebrows are self-evidently insane. The incompleteness IS the joke.
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn famously has spectacular eyebrows — this is a visual gag embedded in dialogue. The trailing off works beautifully because no further description is needed. Economy score is high because the incomplete sentence is funnier than anything he could have said.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hey, listen, I just feel bad for that maid I had fired. That's right, it was coke.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: I was balling that maid-- And oh, don't worry about her, man. She had the time of her life.

jokes.text: Stan: 'I can't pick up a magazine without reading your name these days. I was just reading about you in The Star. You drink cranberry juice.'
jokes.setup: Stan is complimenting Larry on his fame and visibility
jokes.punchline: The supposed evidence of Larry's stardom — reading about him — turns out to be tabloid trivia about his beverage preferences
jokes.explanation: A nice deflation of celebrity — Stan's 'fame evidence' is the most trivial possible detail. The reveal that reading about Larry in a magazine means knowing his juice preference is a good satirical beat about tabloid celebrity culture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No wonder our room was never cleaned on time.

jokes.text: Larry: 'At least it didn't go to waste.'
jokes.setup: Stan confesses the stolen money went to coke and hookers
jokes.punchline: Larry's dry approval — 'at least it didn't go to waste' — implies that coke and hookers are the ideal use of funds
jokes.explanation: Six words that do everything: forgiveness, complicity, shared nostalgia, and dark humor about addiction — all wrapped in perfect deadpan economy. Very quotable and functions as a complete joke with zero waste.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey, now.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, now, that sounded like you had Tourette's syndrome.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You're right, it was a little too forced, huh?

jokes.text: Larry: 'I just feel bad for that maid I had fired.' / Stan: 'That's right, it was coke. I was banging that maid—' / Stan: 'She had the time of her life.' / Larry: 'No wonder our room was never cleaned on time.'
jokes.setup: Larry expressing guilt about a maid he had fired — implying she was blamed for the missing money
jokes.punchline: Stan reveals he was sleeping with the maid; Larry's punchline about room service being late is perfectly timed dark comedy
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed escalation — each revelation adds a layer. Larry's punchline is earned because it reframes the maid's distraction as a mundane workplace inefficiency, completely eliding the moral problem. Dark but not gratuitous.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I still listen to the I'm Larry, he's Stan album ever couple of months.
Really?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, no. Actually, I lied. My record player broke during the riots.

jokes.text: Hank's 'Hey, now' — Stan: 'Well, now, that sounded like you had Tourette's syndrome.' / Hank: 'You're right, it was a little too forced, huh?'
jokes.setup: Hank blurts his catchphrase 'Hey, now' reflexively upon meeting Stan
jokes.punchline: Stan calls it out as sounding like Tourette's; Hank agrees it was 'a little too forced' — a character acknowledging his own catchphrase is compulsive and hollow
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's strongest joke and one of the show's best Hank moments. The meta-comedy of a character acknowledging that his own signature phrase sounds like a neurological disorder — and then agreeing it was forced — is genuinely sophisticated. It deconstructs the catchphrase as a performance tic, which is both funny and a sharp insight into Hank's hollow showbiz persona. Hank's self-aware capitulation ('you're right, it was a little too forced') makes it even better. Justifies the high score.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey, the old partner meets the new partner.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The ex-partner.

jokes.text: Hank claims to love the 'I'm Larry, He's Stan' album and listens every couple months — then immediately: 'Well, no. Actually, I lied. My record player broke during the riots.'
jokes.setup: Hank is performing enthusiasm for Stan's old work with Larry
jokes.punchline: He immediately recants, blaming the LA riots for why he can't listen to the album — then asking if it's on CD
jokes.explanation: Hank's pattern of performing sincerity then immediately undermining it is character-perfect. Using the LA riots as an excuse for not having a working record player is a brilliantly specific absurdist detail. The CD inquiry suggests he might actually listen if the format were more convenient — which makes the original lie even more pathetic. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Who are we trying to avoid?

jokes.text: Artie: 'Hey, the old partner meets the new partner.' / Hank: 'The ex-partner.'
jokes.setup: Artie introduces the dynamic between Stan and Hank
jokes.punchline: Hank's immediate correction — 'the ex-partner' — is both pedantic and self-protective; he's asserting his position
jokes.explanation: A small but effective character beat — Hank's insecurity about his position displayed in a single word correction. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Who are we trying to avoid?' — upon being told it's the Chrysler meeting
jokes.setup: Artie has been trying to hustle Larry to a meeting with the Chrysler people — standard sponsor management
jokes.punchline: When someone asks about the meeting, Artie's reflexive response is 'who are we trying to avoid' — revealing that meeting-management is just avoidance management
jokes.explanation: A sharp industry insight — the assumption that any meeting is about dodging someone rather than attending. Very Artie, economical, and true to the show's behind-the-scenes cynicism.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'd probably temp.

jokes.text: Larry casually invites Stan to dinner — 'Come over for dinner' — followed by [crickets chirping] sound effect
jokes.setup: Larry makes what sounds like a warm social invitation to his old partner
jokes.punchline: The literal crickets underscore how forced and hollow the invitation is — pure awkward silence comedy
jokes.explanation: The literal cricket sound is an unusually theatrical touch for this show — almost a wink at the audience — but it works because the silence IS the content. The scene transition makes the gap between Larry's offer and the next scene (at dinner) feel both inevitable and dread-inducing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm tired of holding this whole conversation. Would you please say something?

jokes.text: Stan reveals he's 'been working... as a temp.' / Larry's pained: 'Oh, well, that's — that's great.' / Then: 'Isn't it, Larry?' / Larry: 'Great. That is great.'
jokes.setup: The dinner scene — Stan is asked what he's been doing since quitting stand-up
jokes.punchline: The long pause before 'as a temp' — followed by Larry's hollow, over-emphatic assurances that temp work is 'great' — is pure cringe
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders cringe — the 'great, that is great' repeated affirmation is an actor's gift of a line because it says the exact opposite of what's true. The pregnant pause before 'as a temp' is the sad heart of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I just feel so fucking guilty.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I'd probably temp.'
jokes.setup: Discussion about the importance of creative outlets — someone says Larry needs his comedy outlet; what would he do without it?
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat reply: 'I'd probably temp.' — delivered without self-pity or comedy, just honest assessment
jokes.explanation: Three words that contain multitudes. Larry looks at Stan — a man reduced to temp work — and sees his mirror image. The line is delivered with zero flourish, which makes it devastating. It's simultaneously compassionate, terrified, self-aware, and funny. This is the kind of joke that only works in a show this committed to psychological truth. Easily justifies 8.5 — it's the most emotionally resonant comedy beat in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We only use two rooms.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: They're not all ours. I noticed. It's like the shining. I think I saw scatman crothers in your kitchen burning toast.

jokes.text: Stan: 'After Larry left... my life changed a lot.' / Larry's partner's wife: 'I think change can be a very good thing sometimes.'
jokes.setup: Stan begins to implicate Larry in the collapse of his life
jokes.punchline: The friend/wife's chipper, therapeutic non-response — 'change can be a very good thing' — is exactly the wrong thing to say and she knows it
jokes.explanation: The inappropriately upbeat platitude in the face of someone's ruined life is a reliable cringe-comedy beat. Functional but not exceptional — we've seen this move before.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Temp worker, my ass. He's a stone hustler.

jokes.text: Stan excuses himself to find the bathroom — 'It's kind of weird. You have to — you know — all the way through the kitchen, stan.' — and the callback: 'Hey, that was that one New Year's Eve, man.'
jokes.setup: Stan asks for the bathroom in Larry's large house
jokes.punchline: A mysterious New Year's Eve incident is referenced — clearly involving Stan getting lost or having an accident — but never explained, which is funnier
jokes.explanation: The unexplained callback to a New Year's Eve bathroom incident is an effective implied-joke — the audience fills in something humiliating. The fact that both Stan and Larry know exactly what it means (and the audience doesn't) creates a funny exclusion.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You've just stepped in a huge pile of shit named Stan Paxton. You're tracking it all over my office.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I'm tired of holding this whole conversation. Would you please say something? God, what do you want me to say to a guy who just says I ruined his life?'
jokes.setup: Larry and his dinner companion in private while Stan is in the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Larry's panic at Stan's implication — 'I ruined his life' — which he apparently heard very clearly despite Stan's elliptical phrasing
jokes.explanation: Larry's anxiety spiral is very character-specific — the way he's already processed Stan's coded accusation and is now freaking out about it is very him. The switch from 'holding the conversation' to 'he ruined my life' is a nice comic escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It's your show, it's my office!

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No. It's your show, It's my office!

jokes.text: Larry: 'I don't feel guilty.' / Francine: 'You shouldn't.' / Larry: 'I just feel so fucking guilty.'
jokes.setup: Francine tells Larry not to feel guilty about Stan's situation
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately contradicts his own denial — the 'fucking' adds emphasis to the reversal
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry self-contradiction — the structure of deny/confirm in rapid succession is a beautifully efficient character revelation. The 'fucking' is perfectly placed. The joke also functions as a diagnostic of Larry's psychology: he can't even maintain a lie to himself for three seconds. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It's your show, it's my office!

jokes.text: Stan: 'It's like The Shining. I think I saw Scatman Crothers in your kitchen burning toast.'
jokes.setup: Stan returns from finding the bathroom in Larry's enormous house
jokes.punchline: The Shining reference is a specific and funny pop culture joke — but the detail of 'Scatman Crothers burning toast' (the cook character in The Shining) is the elevated element
jokes.explanation: A strong pop-culture joke that earns its reference — not just name-dropping The Shining but specifying Scatman Crothers and the mundane detail of 'burning toast' instead of axe murder. The mundane version of horror is funnier than the obvious reference.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: I got into this mainly to get laid. I think that's what basically bothered Larry was that I was getting laid all the time.

jokes.text: Larry offers Stan a full-time writing job — Stan immediately asks: 'What would it pay?'
jokes.setup: Larry makes a spontaneous, guilt-driven offer of a TV writing job
jokes.punchline: Stan's beat of silence followed by salary question — the idealism of the offer immediately deflated by Stan's practical mercenary response
jokes.explanation: The pause before the salary question is the joke — the beat between gratitude and calculation. The transcript marks it with blank space at 08:42, suggesting a significant beat. The mercenary question after the apparent emotional moment is character-specific to Stan.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: Just get me the newspapers, capisce?

jokes.text: Artie: 'I should have been at that dinner.' / Artie: 'Temp worker, my ass. He's a stone hustler.'
jokes.setup: Artie hears that Stan immediately asked about pay after being offered the job
jokes.punchline: Artie's cynicism is vindicated — 'stone hustler' is a great insult delivered with conviction
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'stone hustler' is a great phrase — it has a '70s private-eye quality that's very Artie. His certainty is funny because he was right, but also because he was ready to write Stan off immediately. The 'temp worker, my ass' dismissal is very Rip Torn.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: Yeah, the one about the comic who comes to town, fucks the princess.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Could we try not be so cynical?' / Artie: 'I'm being realistic, buddy. You've just stepped in a huge pile of shit named Stan Paxton. You're tracking it all over my office.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks Artie to give Stan a chance
jokes.punchline: Artie's elaborate shit metaphor — the tracking of it through 'my office' — is both vivid and a territorial assertion
jokes.explanation: Artie's metaphors have a specific poetic vulgarity that's one of the show's great pleasures. 'Stepped in a huge pile of shit named Stan Paxton' is memorable and the 'tracking it all over my office' extension adds territorial comedy. The 'my office' correction (vs. 'our office') is also a nice power-assertion beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The water here in los angeles is so bad, the lead content is so high, that it was announced today a baby was born in los angeles hospital who weighed 7,000 pounds.

jokes.text: Larry: 'It's our office, Artie.' / Artie: 'No. It's your show, it's my office!'
jokes.setup: Larry corrects Artie's possessive claim about 'my office'
jokes.punchline: Artie's paradoxical logic: Larry's show, Artie's office — a territorial division that makes its own internal sense
jokes.explanation: A great Artie line — the division of ownership is illogical but feels completely true to the character dynamic. Artie's executive producer power is expressed through office possession, not show credit. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He should give the crowd a fucking receipt.

jokes.text: Stan about why he and Larry split: 'I got into this mainly to get laid. I think that's what basically bothered Larry — was that I was getting laid all the time.'
jokes.setup: Jerry asks why Stan and Larry broke up their act — expecting 'creative differences'
jokes.punchline: Stan's cheerfully honest answer: he got into comedy for sex, and Larry was bothered by his success at it
jokes.explanation: Stan's honest explanation of his motivations for entering show business — and the suggestion that Larry was jealous rather than principled — is a sharp character reveal. The inversion of the expected 'creative differences' answer is the joke's engine.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: Who do I blow around here to get my jokes on?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Me.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Me.

jokes.text: Stan: 'Anyway, I was balling the chicks everywhere we went. And Larry, basically, would fall in love everywhere. I think that's how he met Francine. Oh, it's like a fairy tale.' / Jerry: 'Yeah, the one about the comic who comes to town, fucks the princess.'
jokes.setup: Stan is telling the origin story of Larry meeting Francine — framing it as romantic
jokes.punchline: Jerry's reframe of it as a crude fairy tale — 'fucks the princess' — subverts the romantic framing with maximum bluntness
jokes.explanation: Jerry's punchline is sharp — the fairy-tale setup and the crude biological restatement creates a good contrast. The structure works because Stan's setup is genuinely romantic-sounding, making the deflation more effective.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Drinking during the monologue at my fucking monitor. You're kidding. Are you positive? I could smell it in his coffee-- some kind of cheap, domestic plain-wrapped vodka.

jokes.text: Stan's monologue joke about a baby in LA weighing 7,000 pounds due to lead content in the water — the writers' room reaction: 'Yeah. He sold it. He sold it well.' / Artie: 'He should give the crowd a fucking receipt.'
jokes.setup: The writers are watching Stan's joke get performed on air — it's a mediocre joke
jokes.punchline: Artie's reaction — 'he should give the crowd a fucking receipt' — implies the audience bought something worthless
jokes.explanation: 'He should give the crowd a fucking receipt' is genuinely exceptional showbiz-insider comedy. The metaphor is perfect: the audience has 'purchased' entertainment and been cheated. It's a writer's room critique compressed into a devastating retail metaphor. Very Artie — the combination of business language and profanity is his signature. Easily justifies the 8.0 score.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's for weekends. I'll talk to stan. I got to piss. I've got to go alone. I've got to clear my head, all right?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'll just hang here by the door like some crapper gargoyle.

jokes.text: Stan watching the monitor: 'He skipped another of my jokes. What are you saving it for, Larry, the Tonys?'
jokes.setup: Larry is dropping Stan's submitted jokes from the monologue
jokes.punchline: The Tonys reference — theatrical awards for Broadway — is the wrong awards show for a TV comedian, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: The Tonys reference is a nice choice — it's not the Emmys or even the Grammys, it's theatre awards, which is absurdist overkill. The frustration of the comedy writer watching his material get dropped is relatable industry humor.

dialogue.line: You're in a bathroom. You smell disinfectant and urine.

jokes.text: Stan: 'Who do I blow around here to get my jokes on?' / Both writers simultaneously: 'Me.'
jokes.setup: Stan, frustrated that his jokes aren't being used, asks rhetorically who he needs to sexually service to get airtime
jokes.punchline: Both writers respond simultaneously and sincerely with 'Me' — the spontaneous chorus of sexual offers
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it's instant and unanimous — the writers don't even confer. The simultaneous delivery is the structural key; one person saying 'Me' is a mild joke, both saying it together is genuinely funny because it implies they've been waiting for this question. Perfect economy — one word each, maximum laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: What is this, your office, fonzie?

jokes.text: Stan: 'Stan, shut the fuck up.' — Artie ordering Stan to silence himself
jokes.setup: Stan is continuing to complain about his jokes being skipped
jokes.punchline: Artie's command is abrupt, profane, and completely non-negotiable — followed by 'Thank you.'
jokes.explanation: Very Artie — the bluntness is the joke, and the 'Thank you' following the shutdown is beautifully poised. The manners after the profanity is a classic Artie move. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: There's nothing I like better after a big meal than spinning around till I puke.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I won't tolerate alcohol in my office.' / Beverly: 'You have alcohol in your office.' / Larry: 'That's for weekends.'
jokes.setup: Larry makes a principled stand against alcohol in the workplace
jokes.punchline: Beverly immediately punctures the hypocrisy; Larry's rationalization ('that's for weekends') is a perfect shameless double-standard
jokes.explanation: A three-line perfect joke. The hypocrisy setup, the puncturing, and the completely unashamed rationalization — 'that's for weekends' — is a great punchline because Larry doesn't even attempt to justify it properly. He just redraws the line. High structure, high character integration, very quotable. Justifies 8.0.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Larry is going to be an honorary silent partner. You think you can handle it?

jokes.text: Artie: 'I've got to go alone. I've got to clear my head, all right?' / Beverly: 'I'll just hang here by the door like some crapper gargoyle.'
jokes.setup: Artie needs to talk to Larry privately and is heading to the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Beverly's 'crapper gargoyle' self-description — announcing she'll stand by the bathroom door is a surreal and vivid image
jokes.explanation: 'Crapper gargoyle' is a genuinely original and vivid phrase — one of those coinages that feels inevitable once you hear it but you'd never have thought of it. The image of Beverly stoically stationed at a bathroom door like a medieval stone monster is hilarious. Very quotable. The originality score is high because this kind of specific, visual insult-of-self is rare. Justifies 8.2.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: One what?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Uh, table.

jokes.text: Larry confronts Stan about drinking in a public bathroom. Stan: 'You're in a bathroom. You smell disinfectant and urine.' / Larry: 'How come I smell it on your breath?'
jokes.setup: Larry accuses Stan of smelling like alcohol; Stan gestures at the bathroom as an alternative explanation
jokes.punchline: Larry's logical follow-up — if it's just bathroom smell, why is it on your breath — is a neat trap
jokes.explanation: The bathroom-as-alibi is a nice comic structure — Stan's deflection is almost logical for a beat, then Larry closes the trap. The scene is darker than it is funny but the exchange has good architecture.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: Hank, that'd be like me asking you to say 'hey, now.'

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Ok. Hey, now.

jokes.text: Stan complains about 'Frick and Frack out there' burying his jokes and asks to bring material directly to Larry — Larry agrees — Stan: 'What is this, your office, Fonzie?'
jokes.setup: Larry and Stan are having a private conversation in a bathroom stall — Larry agrees to look at Stan's jokes
jokes.punchline: Stan's 'Fonzie' reference implies Larry is holding court in a men's room the way Fonzie held court in his bathroom office on Happy Days
jokes.explanation: The Fonzie comparison is apt and specific — both Larry and Fonzie have their bathrooms as power centers. The reference works because it's exactly right and slightly deflating. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Maybe if you'd told him that back then, they maybe today Stan would be Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's horrible thing to say. I wouldn't wish that on anybody.

jokes.text: Artie (watching the Hank restaurant pitch): 'Fuck me. Someone just fuck me right now.'
jokes.setup: Artie is watching some kind of terrible business pitch or promotional segment
jokes.punchline: Artie's invocation of self-directed sexual violence as an expression of despair — delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: This is a quintessential Artie line — the escalation from 'fuck me' to 'someone just fuck me right now' implies such profound professional suffering that only immediate sexual violation would be appropriate. Very Rip Torn, very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Fucking crime to-- you don't ruin a beautiful piece of meat.

jokes.text: Hank pitches 'Hank's Look-Around Cafe' — a restaurant with spinning tables — Larry: 'There's nothing I like better after a big meal than spinning around till I puke.'
jokes.setup: Hank is pitching a restaurant concept that presumably involves some spinning or rotating feature
jokes.punchline: Larry's deadpan summary of the experience — spinning until vomiting — as 'nothing I like better'
jokes.explanation: Larry's deadpan critique is nicely constructed — phrased as enthusiasm ('nothing I like better') while describing a nightmare. The specificity of 'spinning around till I puke' is funnier than a gentler critique would be.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: You owe me this one, Larry. Come on. You know that. You owe me this one.

jokes.text: Larry: 'There's nothing I like better after a big meal than spinning around till I puke.'
jokes.setup: Hank explains the rotating table concept
jokes.punchline: Larry's review of the dining experience from the customer's perspective — nausea as the logical outcome
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan demolition of the concept. The fake enthusiasm ('there's nothing I like better') before 'spinning around till I puke' is classically structured irony. Short, efficient, devastating.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: I was down in bakersfield. Is that strange or what? I mean, it's such a boring, boring place. I mean, once you've masturbated, you've pretty much shot the day.

jokes.text: Hank tells Stan: 'You know, you don't have much discretionary income, but I just want you to know that you're always going to have a table waiting for you at Hank's Look-Around Cafe.' / Stan: 'Which one do you want?' / Hank: 'Uh, table.' / Long pause / Stan: 'Ok, I'll take this one.'
jokes.setup: Hank generously offers Stan 'a table' at his future restaurant — the charitable gesture of a delusional celebrity
jokes.punchline: The confusion over what 'which one' means — apparently there's only one table, or Stan is selecting from a floor plan — and the long beat before Stan just accepts it
jokes.explanation: The scene's comedy is in the confusion and the beat — Hank's charity is so muddled that Stan can't even understand what he's being offered. The pause before 'Ok, I'll take this one' is the kind of moment that rewards rewatching. Hank's blunt mention of Stan's poverty ('you don't have much discretionary income') is an un-self-aware addition.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: David koresh--the guy down at waco, texas-- it turns out he was obsessed with madonna. I guess that guy was off his rocker after all.

jokes.text: Hank asks Stan to perform the old 'Man on the Street meets the Man on the Moon' bit. Stan: 'Hank, that'd be like me asking you to say "Hey, now."' / Hank: 'Ok. Hey, now.'
jokes.setup: Stan uses the catchphrase request as an analogy to explain why he won't perform his old bit
jokes.punchline: Hank completely misses the point of the analogy and just performs the catchphrase — Stan's example becomes a live demonstration
jokes.explanation: This is arguably the episode's best joke. The structure is impeccable: Stan uses 'hey, now' as an example of something embarrassing to perform on command — and Hank immediately performs it, completely validating Stan's point while also demonstrating that Hank has no self-awareness about his own catchphrase. It's a callback, a meta-joke, and a character comedy triumph simultaneously. The joke requires knowing Hank well enough to anticipate his obliviousness, and then it exceeds expectations. Justifies the 8.7 score — approaches the 9-range for structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, my guess it that tape did come out of his ass.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I really like you, Stan Paxton.' / Stan: 'Thanks, Hank.' — Beat — the sincerity landing awkwardly in the void
jokes.setup: Hank has been performing affection throughout the scene
jokes.punchline: The declaration lands without irony — and Stan's simple 'Thanks, Hank' accepts it at face value — the emptiness of the exchange IS the joke
jokes.explanation: A quiet beat that works because Hank's affection for Stan is genuine but pointless — the warmth evaporates immediately. Functional cringe/pathos moment rather than a great joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: He almost made abortion funny.

jokes.text: Artie to Larry: 'You don't help alcoholics by giving them everything they want.' / Larry: 'I don't give him everything he wants.' / Artie: 'Why can't you confront people?'
jokes.setup: Artie pressing Larry to confront Stan about his drinking
jokes.punchline: Larry denies giving Stan everything he wants — which is immediately shown to be false — and Artie's question about confrontation is both diagnostic and comic
jokes.explanation: A functional character beat — Artie's direct analysis of Larry's avoidance is both funny and true. The irony of Larry denying something we've just watched him do is gentle hypocrisy comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's all he did was five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It's about five minutes too long.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Maybe if you'd told him that back then, maybe today Stan would be Hank.' / Larry: 'That's a horrible thing to say.' / Artie: 'I wouldn't wish that on anybody.'
jokes.setup: Artie argues that Larry should have confronted Stan about drinking 15 years ago
jokes.punchline: The suggestion that Stan could have risen to Hank's level — and the immediate self-correction that being Hank is not actually something to aspire to
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: positing being Hank as the positive outcome of Stan's recovery — then immediately pulling the rug by confirming that being Hank is itself a kind of ruin. Artie insults Hank without him present, which is the cleanest kind of insult. 'I wouldn't wish that on anybody' is deeply quotable. The character integration is exceptional — only Artie can deliver this with the right mix of sincerity and malice. Justifies 8.5 easily.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Like who?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Gallagher. We haven't had gallagher on, but there's a perfect example.

jokes.text: Artie about the steaks: 'Fucking crime to — you don't ruin a beautiful piece of meat.' / Then: 'Artie, I'm firing Stan tomorrow.' / Artie: 'Good. Giving a guy like that everything he wants is not helping him.' / Larry: 'I don't give him everything he wants.' / Beverly (off): 'Where is the beer?'
jokes.setup: Artie is outraged by an overcooked steak; then Larry makes a principled decision; then immediately someone requests a beer
jokes.punchline: The beer request immediately after Larry declares 'I don't give him everything he wants' — implying the alcohol is already flowing freely
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Larry's principled statement with the immediate beer request is a good structural irony. Artie's steak outrage ('fucking crime') is also a nice character beat — his priorities include quality meat alongside human welfare.

jokes.text: Stan discovers that half the jokes being prepped haven't come through him — they're ones he submitted directly to Larry's office. Stan: 'Has there been a change in procedure?' / Larry: 'There's no change in procedure.' — despite having explicitly agreed to this 10 minutes ago
jokes.setup: Stan is confronting the writers' room about his jokes being bypassed
jokes.punchline: Larry denies creating a new procedure that he himself created — a small, cowardly lie told directly to the person he created it with
jokes.explanation: Larry's instant denial of his own agreement is a perfect character beat — he can't commit to anything and will gaslight anyone to avoid conflict. The rewatch value is high because you know exactly what deal he's denying.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: I've gone onstage like this 100 times.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, I remember. I remember you tripping over the mike stand, insulting people in the audience, and just generally sucking.

jokes.text: Stan's heartfelt speech about how great it is to write jokes 'for real people instead of telling them to a waitress someplace' — then immediately: 'Oh wait. Oh wait a minute. Oh — this is the kiss-off.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to fire Stan gently; Stan gives a sincere speech about the job meaning to him; Larry responds warmly
jokes.punchline: Stan's sudden mid-speech realization that the compliments are a prelude to firing — the veteran showbiz pattern recognition kicking in
jokes.explanation: A great structural moment — Stan's self-awareness mid-speech is both funny and sad. He's been in show business long enough to recognize the pattern of 'your work is great, but...' and immediately names it. The interruption of his own genuine sentiment with mercenary pattern recognition is beautifully written.

dialogue.speaker: Stan
dialogue.line: I've gone onstage like this 100 times. You remember.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, I remember. I remember you tripping over the mike stand, insulting people in the audience, and just generally sucking.

jokes.text: Stan: 'Let me go on the show and do them.' / Larry: 'You haven't been onstage in what — 15 fucking years?' / Stan: 'You owe me this one, Larry. Come on. You know that. You owe me this one.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to explain why Stan's jokes aren't working for him — Stan's solution is to go on the show himself
jokes.punchline: Stan's doubling down on 'you owe me this one' twice in rapid succession — the naked emotional leverage deployed openly
jokes.explanation: The 'you owe me' gambit is more painful than funny, but the repetition of it twice — the escalating desperation — has comic value. Functional cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Because you're fucking drunk, stan. The same way you were 15 years ago. That's why I left.

jokes.text: Stan: 'I've got tapes coming out of my asshole. You want a tape? I got a tape. I'll go get you a tape. I'll go get you a tape. I'll get tapes.'
jokes.setup: Larry mentions needing to see a tape through proper procedure
jokes.punchline: Stan's frantic, repeated insistence that he has endless tapes — the desperation escalating with each repetition
jokes.explanation: The 'tapes coming out of my asshole' opener is strong; the repeated 'I'll get you a tape' is escalating desperation comedy. Slightly over-extended but the energy is right.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Is he, uh...

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No, he even bungled that. He missed.

jokes.text: Stan's tape: 'Speaking of rehab, I was down in Bakersfield... I mean, it's such a boring, boring place. I mean, once you've masturbated, you've pretty much shot the day.'
jokes.setup: Stan's stand-up tape — he's talking about being in rehab in Bakersfield
jokes.punchline: The assessment that masturbation exhausts the entertainment options in Bakersfield — and the dark implication of what rehab was actually like
jokes.explanation: Stan's tape joke has a nice deadpan quality — the Bakersfield premise is the setup, the masturbation-as-entertainment punchline is earned. Also works as character backstory: Stan has apparently been in rehab, which retroactively shades everything. Stand-up content.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: They found him in his car.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What do you mean, they found him?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He was shot.

jokes.text: Stan's tape: 'David Koresh — the guy down at Waco, Texas — it turns out he was obsessed with Madonna. I guess that guy was off his rocker after all.'
jokes.setup: Stan's Koresh/Waco joke — the setup implies the cult leader's crimes weren't proof enough of insanity
jokes.punchline: The Madonna obsession is what finally confirms he was 'off his rocker' — a deliberate inversion of what's actually crazy
jokes.explanation: A solid topical joke — the inversion of what qualifies as madness (mass murder is debatable; Madonna fandom seals it) is a clean structure. Dated but well-constructed. Stand-up content.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He shot off the top of his left ear. My god, my god, my god. Stan killed himself. He didn't kill himself. He just fucked up his left ear.

jokes.text: [Stan's tape ends — Larry turns off the TV] / Artie: 'Well, my guess is that tape did come out of his ass.'
jokes.setup: Stan claimed to have tapes 'coming out of his asshole'; they've now watched one
jokes.punchline: Artie's callback to the 'asshole' boast — confirmed by the quality of the tape
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback with beautiful economy. The joke pays off Stan's earlier claim by suggesting the tape's quality matches its stated origin. Artie's 'my guess is' adds a lawyerly precision that makes it funnier. One of Artie's best one-liners in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: And he had a shotgun. He put a shotgun in his mouth and he pulled the trigger. Why would anybody do anything like that?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Bullshit! It was his ear.

jokes.text: Phil: 'He blows.' / Pause / 'I mean, but he almost made abortion funny.'
jokes.setup: The staff is assessing Stan's tape
jokes.punchline: 'Almost made abortion funny' — the specific and unexpected subject matter of Stan's set implies he swung for very dark material and nearly landed it
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most surprising and quotable lines. The specificity of 'abortion' as the subject matter Stan nearly made funny is both a critique (he chose the hardest possible target) and a backhanded compliment. The faint praise structure — 'he blows... BUT he almost made abortion funny' — is brilliantly constructed. High originality because no one expects this specific punchline. Justifies 8.0.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: This is a horrible trick. He's talking to him, Hank. Maybe yes, maybe no.

jokes.text: Jerry: 'He looked good.' — as a positive review of the tape
jokes.setup: Staff scrambling for something positive to say about Stan's clearly weak tape
jokes.punchline: The best anyone can offer is that Stan's physical appearance on camera was acceptable
jokes.explanation: Three words that define the damning-with-faint-praise genre. After 'he blows' and 'almost made abortion funny,' the best endorsement available is 'he looked good.' Perfect economy — no more words needed.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Don't you have to be working longer than three days to qualify for the health plan?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Artie!

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No health plan!

jokes.text: Larry: 'We haven't had Gallagher on, but there's a perfect example.' — as an example of 'worse comics than this'
jokes.setup: The group is trying to justify putting Stan on — 'we've had worse comics than this on'
jokes.punchline: The example of 'worse' is a comic they've never actually had on — making Gallagher the hypothetical floor of quality
jokes.explanation: The Gallagher joke has a nice twist — the example of worse comedy is someone they haven't booked, implying they were actually keeping the floor higher than Gallagher. It's also a period-specific industry dig that feels real.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Fuck it. Let's put him on.' / Then: 'All right.' / Then: 'We can't put him on.' / Artie: 'Damn right we can't.'
jokes.setup: The group debates putting Stan on; Larry makes a decision
jokes.punchline: Larry reverses course within about 30 seconds — both decisions delivered with equal conviction
jokes.explanation: Larry's decision reversal in under a minute is a perfect character beat — he's constitutionally incapable of commitment and both his 'Fuck it' and 'We can't' are delivered with total conviction. Artie's immediate 'Damn right we can't' following the reversal is the correct response.

jokes.text: [Sound of bottle clattering] — Stan is discovered with alcohol in his dressing room before going on
jokes.setup: Larry goes to check on Stan before the show
jokes.punchline: The bottle clattering — the sound of Stan caught drinking — makes explicit what everyone feared
jokes.explanation: The sound gag works economically — the clatter tells us everything before dialogue confirms it. Not a great joke in isolation but narratively perfect and has rewatch value as the moment the episode's central conflict becomes undeniable.

jokes.text: [A bottle clatters offscreen; Stan is found clearly drunk in his dressing room]
jokes.setup: Larry goes to find Stan before the show; we've been told he's been drinking
jokes.punchline: The bottle clattering sound precedes Stan's appearance, immediately confirming everything without words
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed sound gag — the bottle clatter does the work of an entire scene of exposition. The humor here is dark (the situation is genuinely sad) but the timing is efficient and cinematic. Not a ha-ha laugh but a knowing chuckle.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I remember you tripping over the mike stand, insulting people in the audience, and just generally sucking.' / Stan: 'We can go back and forth on this all night.'
jokes.setup: Stan says he's gone onstage drunk 100 times; Larry: 'You remember'
jokes.punchline: Larry's specific, comprehensive list of Stan's drunk-onstage failures — delivered as a memory rather than a critique; Stan's undefended acceptance
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'tripping over the mike stand, insulting people in the audience, and just generally sucking' paints a vivid picture. Stan's 'we can go back and forth on this all night' is a funny non-rebuttal — he doesn't dispute any of it, he just declines to continue the accounting.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Is he, uh...' / Larry: 'No, he even bungled that. He missed. He shot off the top of his left ear.' / [Snickers]
jokes.setup: Larry learns that Stan shot himself — the news delivered as tragedy
jokes.punchline: Artie's laugh — a snicker at 'he even bungled that' — the darkest possible punchline delivered with a laugh that he immediately seems to regret
jokes.explanation: The darkest joke in the episode — and one of the bravest choices in the script. 'He even bungled that' applies the comedy of Stan's professional incompetence to his suicide attempt. The snicker is the key: Artie catches himself finding it funny. This is exactly the kind of moral complexity the show does better than anyone else. Justifies the 8.4 score — not quite legendary, but genuinely exceptional dark comedy.

jokes.text: Hank's competing versions: ear vs. shotgun — 'I have friends at Memorial Hospital. He put a shotgun in his mouth and pulled the trigger.' / Artie: 'Bullshit! It was his ear.' / Hank: 'What friends?'
jokes.setup: The group debates the details of Stan's suicide attempt — Artie says it was his ear, Hank insists it was a shotgun in his mouth
jokes.punchline: Artie's demand for Hank to name his hospital sources — the absurdity of fact-checking the horror story
jokes.explanation: The debate over the specifics of a suicide attempt is classic Larry Sanders tonal agility — treating a horror as an information dispute. Artie's 'What friends?' demanding Hank name his hospital sources is the right escalation. Dark, character-specific, and perfectly calibrated to the show's sensibility.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I don't think so.' — repeated twice, insisting Stan cannot be on the phone because he just shot himself
jokes.setup: Beverly says Stan is on the phone from the hospital; Larry takes the call
jokes.punchline: Hank's obstinate 'I don't think so / Maybe yes, maybe no' despite the evidence of Larry visibly talking to Stan
jokes.explanation: Hank doubling down on his incorrect version even while Larry is clearly on the phone with Stan is great character comedy. His 'maybe yes, maybe no' is a hilarious retreat from certainty while still not fully conceding. Very Hank.

jokes.text: Larry on the phone with Stan: 'Well, I guess you could fax them right here.' / Stan apparently wants to fax jokes from the hospital
jokes.setup: Larry is on the phone with Stan who just attempted suicide
jokes.punchline: Stan is apparently already trying to get his jokes to Larry from the hospital — back to work mode immediately
jokes.explanation: The dark comedy of a man who just attempted suicide immediately pivoting to faxing jokes from the hospital is both funny and desperately sad. It also characterizes Stan perfectly — his identity is entirely wrapped up in the work. The way Larry accommodates this ('well, I guess you could fax them right here') without questioning it is very him.

jokes.text: Stan asks about health insurance. Larry asks Artie. Artie shouts: 'No health plan!' [Door slams.] / Larry: 'Uh, stan, I guess there's some procedure.'
jokes.setup: Stan asks from the hospital whether his health care is covered — he's been on the job three days
jokes.punchline: Artie's emphatic 'No health plan!' followed by a door slam — bureaucratic logic applied to a man recovering from a self-inflicted gunshot wound; Larry's mealy-mouthed 'I guess there's some procedure'
jokes.explanation: The perfect ending to the episode. Artie's 'No health plan!' is the funniest possible bureaucratic response to a suicide survivor's hospital bills. The door slam punctuates it like a rimshot. Larry's 'I guess there's some procedure' is the ideal coward's translation. The joke earns its place because the buildup is all there — we've watched Stan unravel for 24 minutes and the final joke is that the system won't even cover the wreckage. Justifies 8.5 craft / 9.0 impact — the episode's final image is this joke landing.

tmdb_overview: Larry reluctantly agrees to hire his former comedy partner as a show writer.
